equipment.name: PMP and PP-2005M pontoon parks
equipment.role: River crossing equipment
equipment.description: Truck-carried pontoon sections that unfold into a floating bridge. The failed crossing of the Siverskyi Donets near Bilohorivka in May 2022, where Ukrainian artillery caught a Russian force on and around a pontoon bridge, destroyed most of a battalion tactical group's vehicles and became the standing illustration of how hard opposed crossings are under drone observation.

equipment.name: MTU-72 and TMM-6 bridgelayers
equipment.role: Assault and gap-crossing bridges
equipment.description: Armoured bridgelayers that drop a span across a ditch or stream for an assault, and truck-mounted TMM sets that build a longer bridge behind the line. Ukrainian defences dig anti-tank ditches precisely to force their use, and drones wait for them.

equipment.name: Biber bridgelayers and Dachs engineer vehicles
equipment.role: Armoured bridging and engineer support
equipment.description: German-supplied Biber bridgelayers put a span over a gap under fire, and Dachs armoured engineer vehicles dig, clear and recover with a crew under armour. Both appear on the German government's published list of deliveries to Ukraine.

equipment.name: The Surovikin line
equipment.role: Prepared defensive belts and obstacles
equipment.description: The belts of anti-tank ditches, dragon's teeth, trenches and dense minefields dug across Zaporizhzhia and Kherson from late 2022, named in reporting after General Sergei Surovikin. Together with helicopters and drones they stopped Ukraine's 2023 counter-offensive in the first belt, and they are the clearest evidence that Russia learned to prepare ground.

equipment.name: The 2024 fortification programme
equipment.role: State-funded defensive lines
equipment.description: After criticism that positions behind the front were not prepared, Ukraine funded a national fortification programme in 2024 for Donetsk, Kharkiv and Sumy. Ukrainian audits, journalists and soldiers have reported delays, positions built too far back or in the wrong places, and procurement scandals alongside the lines that were built.

equipment.name: ISDM Zemledeliye
equipment.role: Remote mining system
equipment.description: A rocket launcher that lays a minefield instead of firing explosives at a target: it can seed mines across a road, a crossing site or the ground behind an advancing unit within minutes. It turns mining from an engineering task into an artillery one.

equipment.name: PFM-1 Lepestok and POM-3 mines
equipment.role: Scatterable anti-personnel mines
equipment.description: The PFM-1 petal mine, small, green and shaped like a leaf, was scattered into Izium and other occupied towns; Human Rights Watch documented its use in inhabited areas. The POM-3 uses a seismic sensor to detect a walking person and jumps before exploding. Both are banned for Ukraine under the Ottawa Convention, which Russia never joined.

equipment.name: RAAM artillery-delivered mines
equipment.role: Remote anti-armour mining
equipment.description: 155mm shells that scatter anti-tank mines, used to close a gap in front of an armoured assault without sending engineers forward. The United States also approved the transfer of anti-personnel mines in late 2024, a decision criticised by campaigners because Ukraine is a party to the Ottawa Convention and later moved to withdraw from it.

equipment.name: UR-77 Meteorit
equipment.role: Mine-clearing line charge vehicle
equipment.description: Fires a rocket that drags an explosive hose across a minefield and detonates it, blasting a lane. In this war it has been used at least as often to demolish buildings in urban assaults, a practice recorded repeatedly in Russian footage from Bakhmut and elsewhere.

equipment.name: Uran-6 and IMR-3M
equipment.role: Demining robot and armoured engineer vehicle
equipment.description: The small tracked Uran-6 flails ground ahead of troops by remote control; the IMR-3M is a tank-based engineer vehicle with a dozer blade and a crane that clears rubble and obstacles under armour. Both predate the war and both are scarce relative to the frontage.

equipment.name: M58 MICLIC, ploughs and rollers
equipment.role: Breaching equipment for assault lanes
equipment.description: Line charges fired across a minefield, and ploughs and rollers bolted to the front of tanks. Shortages of this unglamorous equipment, and of the training to use it under fire, were among the reasons the 2023 counter-offensive stalled in the first Russian minefield belt.

equipment.name: Bozena, MV-4 and Armtrac demining machines
equipment.origin: Slovakia, Croatia and the United Kingdom
equipment.role: Route and humanitarian demining
equipment.description: Remote-controlled flail and tiller machines donated for clearing roads, fields and returned territory. The scale is the problem: Ukrainian and United Nations statements describe one of the most heavily mined countries in the world and a clearance task measured in decades and billions of dollars.

equipment.name: KamAZ Mustang and Ural trucks
equipment.role: Military cargo trucks
equipment.description: The trucks that carry Russian shells, fuel and food. Early in the war their loss to ambushes exposed how thin Russian logistics were; now the threat is FPV and bomber drones watching every approach road, which has pushed supply runs to night, to dispersal and to smaller vehicles.

equipment.name: Motorcycles, quad bikes and Desertcross buggies
equipment.role: Light assault and resupply transport
equipment.description: From 2024 Russian units increasingly attacked and resupplied on motorcycles, quad bikes and Chinese Desertcross 1000-3 buggies, because armoured vehicles are found and killed by drones before they arrive. It is cheap, fast and appalling for the rider: Ukrainian and Russian footage of motorcycle assaults is abundant.

equipment.name: Donated trucks and tank transporters
equipment.role: Cargo, fuel and heavy equipment transport
equipment.description: FMTV and HEMTT military trucks, European commercial lorries and heavy equipment transporters that move tanks to and from repair. Sustaining donated Western vehicles requires this fleet as much as the vehicles themselves, and it is rarely counted in headline aid figures.

equipment.name: Pickups and volunteer vehicles
equipment.origin: Japan, Europe and the United States (donated)
equipment.role: Last-mile transport for drone crews and ammunition
equipment.description: Second-hand pickups, vans and 4x4s bought by volunteer foundations and driven to the front, where they move drone teams, batteries, water and wounded over the last few kilometres. Losses to FPV drones are heavy and constant, and replacing them is a permanent fundraising campaign.

equipment.name: Sea mines in the Black Sea
equipment.role: Moored and drifting sea mines
equipment.description: Mines laid in the north-western Black Sea from 2022 closed shipping lanes and threatened the grain corridor. Drifting mines washed up on the Turkish, Romanian and Bulgarian coasts and were destroyed by national navies; Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria set up a joint mine countermeasures group in 2024. Each side blames the other for the drifting mines, and attribution of individual mines is rarely possible.

equipment.name: Ukrainian coastal minefields
equipment.role: Defensive mining of the approaches to Odesa
equipment.description: Ukraine mined the approaches to Odesa and the Dnipro-Buh estuary in 2022 against an amphibious landing that never came. The minefields also helped close Ukraine's own ports until the grain corridor arrangements, and clearing them is a condition of normal shipping returning.

equipment.name: K-300P Bastion-P and Bal
equipment.role: Coastal anti-ship missile systems
equipment.description: Mobile launchers in Crimea and Krasnodar carrying Oniks and Kh-35 missiles. They are anti-ship systems used mostly against land targets in this war, including strikes on Odesa, and they have been hit repeatedly by ATACMS and naval drones because their positions are known.

equipment.name: Murmansk-BN
equipment.role: Long-range shortwave jamming complex
equipment.description: A truck-mounted complex with masts tens of metres high that jams high-frequency radio over very long distances, claimed by its maker to reach thousands of kilometres. It is deployed in Crimea and Kaliningrad and is aimed at long-haul military communications rather than at anything on the front line.

equipment.name: Shipovnik-Aero
equipment.role: Counter-drone electronic warfare vehicle
equipment.description: A vehicle-mounted system for finding, jamming and spoofing drone control and video links, credited by Russian sources with taking over drones in flight. Captured examples have been examined by Ukrainian specialists, and it is one of the systems Ukrainian crews try to locate and strike first.

equipment.name: Silok and Repellent-1
equipment.role: Point counter-drone jammers
equipment.description: Jammers built to protect a headquarters, an airfield or a depot rather than a unit in contact: they sweep the control and navigation bands used by small drones. Their effectiveness against fibre-optic drones, which carry no radio link at all, is nil.

equipment.name: Nota and Ai-Petri electronic warfare complexes
equipment.role: Ukrainian jamming and direction finding
equipment.description: Domestically built complexes for jamming Russian communications and drone links and for direction finding. Ukrainian production scaled up sharply from 2023 because donated electronic warfare equipment arrived slowly and the drone problem grew faster.

equipment.name: Trench and vehicle counter-drone jammers
equipment.role: Squad and vehicle protection against FPV drones
equipment.description: Backpack and roof-mounted jammer domes, many from Ukrainian makers such as Kvertus, that put a bubble of interference around a dugout or a pickup. They work against radio-guided FPV drones, interfere with friendly radios and navigation, and do nothing against fibre-optic drones.

equipment.name: Tobol satellite interference complexes
equipment.role: Interference with satellite navigation and satellite links
equipment.description: Fixed complexes reported by Western media, on the basis of leaked United States assessments, to be used against satellite navigation and satellite communications including Starlink. Russia describes Tobol as a system for protecting its own satellites. Public evidence is limited and the entry reflects reporting rather than confirmation.

equipment.name: Pokrova
equipment.role: National satellite navigation spoofing system
equipment.description: A Ukrainian system announced by officials in 2024 that broadcasts false satellite navigation signals to push Shahed-type drones and guided bombs off course over a wide area. Its effect is disputed, it degrades civilian navigation across the same airspace, and independent assessment is not possible from public sources.

equipment.name: Himera G1 radios
equipment.role: Jam-resistant tactical handheld radios
equipment.description: Ukrainian frequency-hopping handhelds designed after 2022 for a jammed battlefield and priced so that a company can be issued them rather than a headquarters. Encrypted Western radios remain scarce, so cheap domestic radios matter more than they should.

equipment.name: R-168 Akveduk and civilian handhelds
equipment.role: Tactical radios and unencrypted commercial sets
equipment.description: The R-168 family is the Russian army's standard tactical radio, but shortages and unfamiliarity pushed units onto unencrypted commercial handhelds bought on the civilian market. Ukrainian electronic warfare and volunteer intercept groups have harvested Russian traffic from these radios throughout the war.

equipment.name: Strelets reconnaissance and control sets
equipment.role: Target data from scouts to artillery
equipment.description: A soldier-carried set that passes coordinates, images and orders between reconnaissance teams, commanders and artillery or Iskander batteries. It is the Russian answer to the problem Ukraine solved with Kropyva and Delta, and it is the link that makes a spotted target into a strike.

equipment.name: S-350 Vityaz
equipment.role: Medium-range surface-to-air system
equipment.description: A newer medium-range system carrying many 9M96 missiles per launcher, intended to relieve S-400 batteries of drone and cruise missile work. Fielded from 2019 and reported in combat use in this war; several launchers have been claimed destroyed by Ukrainian strikes.

equipment.name: FrankenSAM hybrids
equipment.role: Western missiles fired from Soviet launchers
equipment.description: Improvised systems that marry Western missiles to Soviet launchers and radars, the best known firing RIM-7 Sea Sparrow missiles from a Buk launcher. They exist because Ukraine has Soviet launchers and no Soviet missiles left to fire from them, and because Western launchers are scarce.

equipment.name: Su-24M and Su-25
equipment.role: Strike and close air support aircraft
equipment.description: The Su-24M is the aircraft that carries Storm Shadow and SCALP-EG cruise missiles, modified in Ukraine to do so; the Su-25 flies lofted rocket attacks at treetop height because anything higher is inside Russian air defence. Both types are Soviet-built, irreplaceable and steadily lost.

equipment.name: Saab ASC 890
equipment.role: Airborne early warning and control aircraft
equipment.description: Sweden announced the donation of two ASC 890 radar aircraft in 2024. They give Ukraine its own airborne radar picture at altitude, which matters for the F-16 force and for seeing low-flying missiles and drones earlier than ground radar can.

equipment.name: 2S1 Gvozdika, 2S3 Akatsiya and 2S5
equipment.role: Soviet self-propelled howitzers
equipment.description: The Soviet-designed guns that still make up a large part of Ukraine's artillery park, kept firing by donated Polish, Bulgarian, Czech and Greek stocks and by Ukrainian overhaul plants. They are less accurate and shorter-ranged than the Western guns that get the attention, and there are many more of them.

equipment.name: FH70, L119 and Soviet towed guns
equipment.role: Towed howitzers of mixed calibre
equipment.description: Italian and British FH70 and L119 guns, American M101s and Soviet D-20, D-30 and 2A65 pieces, all in service at once. Mixed calibres and mixed ammunition are a logistic burden Ukraine accepted in 2022 because guns were guns.

equipment.name: BM-27 Uragan and BM-30 Smerch
equipment.role: Heavy rocket artillery
equipment.description: Larger and longer-ranged than the Grad, and frequently fired with cluster warheads. Both types have been documented by human rights organisations in strikes on residential areas, where an unguided salvo over a city block is indiscriminate by nature.

equipment.name: RPO-A Shmel
equipment.role: Infantry thermobaric rocket launcher
equipment.description: A shoulder-fired tube whose rocket carries a thermobaric mixture, used against buildings, dugouts and trench positions. It puts the effect of a small artillery shell in the hands of an assault group, and its use in built-up areas has been widely recorded.

equipment.name: AGM-88 HARM
equipment.role: Anti-radiation missile
equipment.description: Supplied in 2022 and improvised onto Soviet MiG-29 and Su-27 aircraft, a modification American engineers and Ukrainian crews worked out together and one of the more surprising technical results of the war. The missile homes on radar emissions, which forces Russian air defence radars to stay quiet or move.

equipment.name: Kh-31P and Kh-35
equipment.role: Anti-radiation and anti-ship missiles
equipment.description: The Kh-31P hunts radars, which is why Ukrainian air defence crews move their sets after every engagement; the Kh-35 is an anti-ship missile regularly fired at land targets from coastal launchers and aircraft.

equipment.name: Kh-59MK2 and Kh-69
equipment.role: Air-launched stealthy cruise missiles
equipment.description: Smaller and harder to detect than the Kh-101, fired from tactical aircraft rather than bombers. Ukrainian officials and analysts identified the Kh-69 in the strike that destroyed the Trypilska power station in April 2024, a case that showed how thin air defence coverage of the grid had become.

equipment.name: Hrim-2 (Sapsan)
equipment.role: Ukrainian short-range ballistic missile
equipment.description: A Ukrainian ballistic missile programme begun before the full-scale invasion and revived during it. Ukrainian officials said in 2025 that it had been used against targets in Russia and was entering serial production. Those are the manufacturer's and government's claims; independent confirmation of numbers or performance is not available.

equipment.name: Snipex Alligator and T-Rex
equipment.role: 14.5mm anti-materiel rifles
equipment.description: Ukrainian-built rifles firing the heavy 14.5mm round designed for anti-tank rifles, used against observation posts, light vehicles, antennas and parked drones at long range. They are heavy, loud and distinctly Ukrainian: a domestic industry that did not exist at this scale before 2014.

equipment.name: Barrett M107 and Accuracy International rifles
equipment.role: Donated precision and anti-materiel rifles
equipment.description: Western .50 calibre and .338 rifles donated from 2022. A Ukrainian security service sniper claimed a record shot of about 3,800 metres in 2023 with a Ukrainian-built rifle; the claim rests on the service's own footage and has not been independently verified.

equipment.name: SVD, SVDM and Chukavin SVCh
equipment.role: Marksman and sniper rifles
equipment.description: The SVD is the marksman's rifle in every Russian platoon and is older than most of the soldiers carrying it; the SVCh is its intended replacement, seen in small numbers. Ordinary infantry marksmanship matters less in a war decided by drones and artillery, but trench lines are still close enough for it.

equipment.name: ASVK Kord and Orsis T-5000
equipment.role: Anti-materiel and precision rifles
equipment.description: The 12.7mm ASVK is Russia's heavy anti-materiel rifle; the commercial Orsis T-5000 is used by special units and was bought in numbers by volunteers. Both appear in Russian sniper publicity, which is a poor guide to how much they matter.

equipment.name: BMP-1, BMP-2 and BMP-1TS
equipment.role: Soviet infantry fighting vehicles
equipment.description: Still the most numerous Ukrainian infantry fighting vehicles, topped up by Czech, Polish and Greek donations and by Ukrainian rebuilds such as the BMP-1TS with a modern turret. Thin armour, a 1960s design and a high casualty rate: crews use them as battle taxis that stop short of the objective.

equipment.name: BMD-2, BMD-4M and BTR-D
equipment.role: Airborne infantry fighting vehicles
equipment.description: Light, air-droppable vehicles built for the airborne forces, with armour thin enough to be opened by heavy machine gun fire. The VDV has fought as ordinary infantry since 2022 and lost these vehicles in quantity doing work they were never designed for.

equipment.name: Leopard 1A5
equipment.role: Legacy main battle tank
equipment.description: A 1970s tank with modern fire control, donated in quantity from 2023 after Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands bought back stored vehicles. Its armour is inadequate against modern anti-tank weapons, so Ukrainian crews use it as a mobile gun firing from cover rather than as an assault tank.

forces.name: Supreme Commander-in-Chief
forces.role: The President of Russia commands the armed forces and, by reporting, intervenes in operational decisions down to brigade level.

forces.name: Ministry of Defence
forces.role: Political and industrial direction of the war: mobilisation, procurement and the wartime economy. Andrei Belousov, an economist, replaced Sergei Shoigu in May 2024.
forces.strength: Russia's declared armed forces ceiling rose to 1.5 million service personnel in 2024 (presidential decree); the deployed force in and around Ukraine is estimated by Ukrainian and Western officials at around 600,000 to 700,000.

forces.name: General Staff and Joint Grouping of Forces
forces.role: Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov has commanded the Joint Grouping of Forces in Ukraine since January 2023, succeeding Sergei Surovikin; he was kept on past retirement age in 2025.

forces.name: Groupings of forces
forces.role: The front is divided into named groupings, each built on a military district headquarters and several combined-arms armies: North (Kharkiv and Sumy axes), West (Kupiansk and Lyman), South (Siversk and the Donetsk sector), Centre (Pokrovsk and the western Donetsk axis), East (Vuhledar and the Zaporizhzhia boundary) and Dnepr (Zaporizhzhia and Kherson).

forces.name: Grouping North
forces.role: Formed in 2024 from the Leningrad Military District's forces for the Kharkiv incursion in May 2024, then the defence of Kursk and the Sumy border. Includes the 6th and 11th Armies and the 44th Army Corps.

forces.name: Grouping West
forces.role: Built on the 1st Guards Tank Army and 20th Combined Arms Army, fighting on the Kupiansk, Lyman and Borova axes in Kharkiv and Luhansk oblasts.

forces.name: Grouping Centre
forces.role: The Central Military District's forces, including the 2nd and 41st Combined Arms Armies and later the 51st Army (the former 1st Donetsk Corps), which carried the main effort against Avdiivka in 2024 and Pokrovsk in 2024 and 2025.

forces.name: Grouping South
forces.role: The Southern Military District's 8th Combined Arms Army with the 3rd Army Corps and the former Luhansk corps, responsible for Bakhmut, Chasiv Yar, Toretsk and Siversk.

forces.name: Grouping East
forces.role: Eastern Military District forces, the 5th, 29th, 35th and 36th Armies, on the Vuhledar and Velyka Novosilka axes at the boundary of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.

forces.name: Grouping Dnepr
forces.role: Holds the Zaporizhzhia front and the left bank of the Dnipro in Kherson with the 58th and 49th Armies and the 18th Army, facing the Ukrainian bridgeheads and the Orikhiv axis.

forces.name: Airborne Forces (VDV)
forces.role: The 7th, 76th, 98th and 106th divisions and separate brigades, used as the mobile reserve and in the heaviest fighting from Hostomel in 2022 to Kursk in 2024 and 2025. Losses have been heavy and units were rebuilt with mobilised soldiers.
forces.strength: Pre-war establishment around 45,000; expanded on paper with new regiments.

forces.name: Naval Infantry
forces.role: The 155th, 40th, 61st and 810th brigades of the fleets' naval infantry, converted to divisions on paper from 2024, fought at Mariupol, Vuhledar and Kursk with repeated heavy losses.

forces.name: Aerospace Forces (VKS)
forces.role: Fighters, Su-34 bombers, the Long-Range Aviation bombers that fire cruise missiles, and the air defence forces. Missile Troops and Artillery and the Iskander brigades sit with the ground forces.

forces.name: Black Sea Fleet
forces.role: Headquartered in Sevastopol until strikes and naval drones forced most ships to Novorossiysk; still launches Kalibr missiles and holds the Kerch Strait.

forces.name: Rosgvardia and Akhmat
forces.role: The National Guard occupies and polices captured territory and fields its own combat units; the Chechen Akhmat formations, formally within Rosgvardia, took Wagner's assault role in some sectors after 2023.

forces.name: Storm-Z and Storm-V penal units
forces.role: Assault units of recruited prisoners attached to regular formations, successors to Wagner's prison recruitment, used for costly infantry attacks along the Donetsk front.

forces.name: North Korean contingent
forces.role: Around 11,000 to 12,000 Korean People's Army troops deployed to Kursk Oblast from late 2024, engaged from November 2024 and reinforced in 2025; North Korea also supplies shells, missiles and guns. Numbers are South Korean, Ukrainian and US estimates.
forces.strength: South Korean intelligence estimated 11,000 deployed by early 2025 plus reinforcements; casualties in the thousands.

forces.name: Supreme Commander-in-Chief
forces.role: The President of Ukraine commands the armed forces through the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief.

forces.name: Ministry of Defence
forces.role: Procurement, mobilisation policy and the defence industry; the ministry changed hands several times during the war and its leadership was contested in the 2026 command crisis.
forces.strength: Ukraine's armed forces number around one million personnel of whom a few hundred thousand serve in combat units, by official statements; exact figures are not published.

forces.name: Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces
forces.role: Oleksandr Syrskyi replaced Valerii Zaluzhnyi in February 2024 and was himself replaced by Mykhailo Drapatyi in July 2026 amid a military leadership crisis (reported structure; confirm against current reporting).

forces.name: General Staff
forces.role: Plans operations and publishes the daily loss claims shown on this page; the Chief of the General Staff post changed hands with the 2024 and 2026 command changes.

forces.name: Ground Forces
forces.role: The largest service: mechanised, motorised, tank, artillery and territorial units. In 2025 brigades were grouped into around 18 army corps in a reform intended to fix the span of control of the earlier operational-tactical groups.

forces.name: Army corps (2025 reform)
forces.role: Corps formed around experienced brigades, including the 1st Azov Corps of the National Guard, the 3rd Army Corps built on the 3rd Assault Brigade, and corps built on the 12th, 53rd and other brigades, each holding a sector with attached artillery and drone units.

forces.name: Operational groupings
forces.role: Regional joint commands over the corps: the eastern grouping (Donetsk and Luhansk fronts, formerly Khortytsia), the southern grouping (Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, formerly Tavria and Dnipro), the Kursk grouping of 2024 and 2025, and the northern border groupings for Sumy and Kharkiv.

forces.name: Air Assault Forces
forces.role: Ukraine's elite light infantry brigades (25th, 79th, 80th, 82nd, 95th and others), used as the fire brigade of the front from Hostomel to Kursk.

forces.name: Unmanned Systems Forces
forces.role: A separate branch created in 2024 for drone units, with dedicated strike regiments such as Magyar's Birds and Achilles that publish confirmed hits; drones now account for the majority of claimed Russian equipment losses.

forces.name: Air Force
forces.role: Fighters (MiG-29, Su-27, F-16, Mirage 2000), Su-24 and Su-25 strike aircraft, and the anti-aircraft missile forces that operate Patriot, SAMP/T, NASAMS and IRIS-T; publishes the nightly interception figures.

forces.name: Navy and Marines
forces.role: Coastal missile batteries, naval drones, small boats and the marine corps brigades that fought at Mariupol and hold the Dnipro delta.

forces.name: Territorial Defence Forces
forces.role: Regional brigades raised in 2022 from volunteers, now fighting as regular infantry across the front; many have been rebuilt several times.

forces.name: Special Operations Forces
forces.role: Raiding, sabotage and long-range reconnaissance inside occupied territory and Russia, alongside Defence Intelligence's own units and naval drone crews.

forces.name: National Guard of Ukraine
forces.role: Interior ministry forces that fight as line units: the National Guard's 1st Azov Corps and other brigades, and the State Border Guard Service's assault units in Kharkiv and Sumy.

forces.name: Defence Intelligence (HUR)
forces.role: The military intelligence directorate runs naval drones, deep strikes and special units and is a frequent source of the claims in this page's updates; treat its statements as an interested party's.

forces.name: Military districts
forces.role: The administrative chain that raises, mans and equips the force, separate from the operational groupings that fight the war. The Western Military District was split back into the Moscow and Leningrad districts in 2024, restoring the five-district layout of the Soviet period.

forces.name: Leningrad Military District
forces.role: Recreated in 2024 out of the Western district, with headquarters in St Petersburg. It generates the forces used on the Kharkiv and Sumy axes and faces the Finnish and Baltic borders after NATO's northern enlargement.

forces.name: Moscow Military District
forces.role: The second half of the 2024 split of the Western district, covering central Russia and the force generation behind the Kupiansk and Lyman axes.

forces.name: Southern Military District
forces.role: Headquartered in Rostov-on-Don, the district that has run the war in Donbas since 2014 and administers occupied Crimea and the southern occupied areas.

forces.name: Central Military District
forces.role: Headquartered in Yekaterinburg; its armies have carried the main effort on the Avdiivka and Pokrovsk axes since 2023.

forces.name: Eastern Military District
forces.role: Headquartered in Khabarovsk; its armies were moved west in 2022 and have fought on the southern Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia boundary ever since.

forces.name: 6th Combined Arms Army
forces.role: A Leningrad district army committed to the Kharkiv incursion of May 2024 and then to holding the Russian side of the Sumy and Kharkiv border.

forces.name: 1st Guards Tank Army
forces.role: Russia's showpiece armoured army before 2022. It lost much of its equipment in the Kharkiv collapse of September 2022, was rebuilt with mobilised soldiers and now fights as ordinary infantry-heavy formations on the Kupiansk axis.

forces.name: 8th Guards Combined Arms Army
forces.role: The Southern district army that absorbed the former Luhansk and Donetsk corps units and fought the long battles for Bakhmut, Chasiv Yar and Toretsk.

forces.name: 51st Combined Arms Army
forces.role: Formed in 2023 from the 1st Army Corps, the former Donetsk separatist force, and folded into the regular army. It fought at Avdiivka and on the Pokrovsk axis.

forces.name: 58th Combined Arms Army
forces.role: Holds the Zaporizhzhia front that absorbed Ukraine's 2023 counter-offensive. Its commander Ivan Popov was dismissed in July 2023 after complaining publicly about counter-battery losses and the treatment of his soldiers.

forces.name: Main Directorate of the General Staff (GRU)
forces.role: Military intelligence: agent networks, the Spetsnaz brigades, deep reconnaissance, and the sabotage campaign in Europe that European security services have attributed to it.

forces.name: Spetsnaz brigades
forces.role: The 2nd, 3rd, 10th, 14th, 16th and 22nd special purpose brigades. Western and Ukrainian reporting says they were used as assault infantry from 2022 and rebuilt repeatedly after heavy losses, well outside their reconnaissance role.

forces.name: Africa Corps
forces.role: The Ministry of Defence structure that took over most of Wagner's African deployments after Yevgeny Prigozhin's death in August 2023, reported to run under General Staff and GRU direction. It fights in the Sahel and Libya rather than in Ukraine, but it absorbed Wagner's people and contracts.
forces.strength: Western and regional reporting put it in the low thousands across Mali, Libya, Burkina Faso and Niger during 2024 and 2025; no official figure is published.

forces.name: Redut and company formations
forces.role: Ministry of Defence-linked contractor structures, Redut chief among them, that recruited Wagner veterans after the 2023 mutiny, alongside state-company units such as Gazprom's Potok. They fight as assault units under regular commanders.

forces.name: Rubicon centre for unmanned systems
forces.role: A drone centre created on the defence minister's order in 2024 to concentrate the best crews, training and equipment. Ukrainian and Western reporting through 2025 described its detachments as the most effective Russian drone units, deployed to Kursk and to the Pokrovsk axis to hunt Ukrainian logistics.

forces.name: Long-Range Aviation
forces.role: The bomber force, Tu-95MS, Tu-160 and Tu-22M3, that launches the cruise missiles in the mass strikes on the power grid and cities. Its home bases, deep inside Russia, have been struck repeatedly by Ukrainian drones, including the June 2025 operation against aircraft parked at several airfields.

forces.name: Missile Troops and Artillery
forces.role: The ground forces' artillery arm, including the Iskander brigades that fire the ballistic and cruise missiles used against cities and airfields.

forces.name: Akhmat formations
forces.role: Chechen units raised under Ramzan Kadyrov, formally inside Rosgvardia and the Ministry of Defence, used for assaults, for blocking detachments behind other units and heavily for publicity. Apty Alaudinov, their public commander, also holds a political post in the Ministry of Defence.

forces.name: Federal Security Service (FSB)
forces.role: Holds the state border with its Border Service, runs counter-sabotage in the border oblasts and places military counter-intelligence officers inside formations. It reports to the president, not to the Ministry of Defence.

forces.name: Eastern grouping of forces
forces.role: The joint command for the Donetsk and Luhansk fronts, previously named Khortytsia. It holds the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka, Siversk and Lyman axes, the heaviest fighting of the war since 2023.

forces.name: Southern grouping of forces
forces.role: The joint command for Zaporizhzhia, Kherson and the Dnipro line, built from the earlier Tavriia and Odesa commands. It also covers the Black Sea coast and the Kinburn spit.

forces.name: Northern grouping of forces
forces.role: Covers Sumy, Chernihiv and northern Kharkiv, the border raids of 2024 and the Kursk operation begun in August 2024, which Russian and North Korean forces largely reversed through the spring of 2025.

forces.name: 3rd Army Corps
forces.role: Built in 2025 around the 3rd Assault Brigade, the formation raised by Andrii Biletskyi from the original Azov Regiment's veterans. It holds part of the Kharkiv and Lyman sector and recruits publicly on its own account.

forces.name: 1st Azov Corps (National Guard)
forces.role: The National Guard corps formed in 2025 around the 12th Azov Brigade, the successor to the Mariupol garrison. It is a National Guard formation that fights under whichever operational grouping holds its sector.

forces.name: 414th Magyar's Birds Brigade
forces.role: The strike drone formation founded by Robert Brovdi, call sign Magyar, which grew from a volunteer unit into the 414th brigade and publishes counted strikes. Brovdi was appointed to command the Unmanned Systems Forces in 2025.

forces.name: 429th Achilles Regiment
forces.role: A strike drone unit grown out of a battalion of the 92nd Brigade into a regiment and then a brigade-sized formation, working the Kharkiv and Donetsk axes and known for publishing verified strike footage.

forces.name: Marine Corps
forces.role: The marine brigades, raised to a corps command in 2023, which fought at Mariupol, held the Krynky bridgehead on the left bank of the Dnipro through 2024 and were committed to the Kursk operation.

forces.name: Air commands and anti-aircraft missile brigades
forces.role: The four regional air commands, Centre, West, South and East, with the anti-aircraft missile brigades, radar brigades and the mobile fire groups that shoot down Shahed-type drones over the cities.

forces.name: Support and logistics forces
forces.role: Engineering, explosive ordnance disposal, chemical defence, movement and supply, plus the Medical Forces. Demining alone is a decades-long task: Ukraine is among the most heavily mined countries in the world by United Nations and government statements.

forces.name: Territorial recruitment centres
forces.role: The conscription and mobilisation offices. Recruitment practice became a public scandal in 2023 to 2025, with corruption cases against centre officials and widely reported complaints about street conscription; mobilisation shortfalls are a recurring theme in Ukrainian and Western reporting.

forces.name: Security Service of Ukraine (SBU)
forces.role: Counter-intelligence and internal security, with its own combat and special operations units: the Alpha special centre, drone units of its 13th directorate and the Sea Baby naval drone programme used against the Kerch bridge and Black Sea Fleet ships.

forces.name: HUR special units
forces.role: Defence Intelligence's own formations, including Tymur, Artan, Shaman, Prymary and the Russian-manned Freedom of Russia and Russian Volunteer Corps units, used for raids into Russia, Crimea and occupied territory.

forces.name: Ministry of Internal Affairs
forces.role: The interior ministry commands the National Guard, the State Border Guard Service and the National Police, all of which field combat formations in this war.

forces.name: State Border Guard Service
forces.role: Border guard detachments and brigades that hold sectors of the front alongside the army, with the Sea Guard and its own aviation.

phases.label: Background, 2014 to 2021
phases.summary: Russia seized Crimea and fostered the war in the Donbas after the Maidan revolution; eight years of trench war followed along a static line while Ukraine rebuilt its army.

phases.label: Full-scale invasion, February to April 2022
phases.summary: Russia attacked from the north, east and south. The drive on Kyiv failed within weeks and Russian forces withdrew from the north, leaving Bucha and Irpin behind them.

phases.label: Battle for the Donbas, April to August 2022
phases.summary: Russia concentrated on the east, took Mariupol, Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk with massed artillery, and was slowed only when HIMARS reached Ukraine.

phases.label: Ukrainian counteroffensives, autumn 2022
phases.summary: Ukraine broke through at Kharkiv and forced the Russian withdrawal from Kherson, while Russia annexed four regions on paper and mobilised 300,000 men.

phases.label: Winter attrition and Bakhmut, late 2022 to mid 2023
phases.summary: Russia struck the power grid all winter and Wagner ground through Bakhmut at enormous cost while both sides prepared for the summer.

phases.label: The 2023 counteroffensive
phases.summary: Ukraine's Western-equipped brigades attacked into deep minefields in Zaporizhzhia and gained little; at sea, naval drones and missiles drove the Black Sea Fleet from Sevastopol.

phases.label: Avdiivka and attrition, 2024
phases.summary: With US aid stalled for months, Russia took Avdiivka with glide bombs and human waves, opened a new front at Kharkiv and ground westward towards Pokrovsk.

phases.label: Kursk and the long-range war, August 2024 to spring 2025
phases.summary: Ukraine invaded Kursk Oblast and held a salient for months against Russian and North Korean troops; deep strikes on refineries and airfields grew on both sides and Russia fired the Oreshnik.

phases.label: Talks, drones and the 2025 summer offensive
phases.summary: Russia's summer offensive made slow, costly gains around Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka while Shahed waves reached record size; the United States pushed peace plans that Kyiv and Europe reworked and Moscow rejected.

The war continued into its fifth year with a slow Russian advance, a growing drone war on both sides, a command crisis in Kyiv in the summer and no ceasefire. Later events appear in the updates feed above.

events.title: The Maidan revolution
events.text: Three months of protest on Kyiv's Independence Square, begun when Viktor Yanukovych refused to sign an association agreement with the European Union, ended with shootings in the city centre and the president's flight to Russia. Parliament voted him out of office on 22 February 2014. Moscow called the change an armed coup and used it to justify what followed.

events.title: Russia seizes Crimea
events.text: Unmarked Russian troops, the little green men, took control of the Crimean parliament and then the peninsula within days of the Maidan revolution. A staged referendum and annexation followed in March. The seizure was the opening of the Russo-Ukrainian war.

events.title: Crimea annexed after a staged referendum
events.text: A referendum held on 16 March under Russian military occupation reported an overwhelming vote to join Russia. Two days later Vladimir Putin signed a treaty of accession in Moscow. Ukraine, the United Nations General Assembly and most member states refused to recognise the annexation, and sanctions on Russia began.

events.title: War begins in the Donbas
events.text: Russian-backed armed groups seized towns in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts; the fighting that followed, including Ilovaisk and Debaltseve, killed some 14,000 people before 2022 and froze into a trench line under the Minsk agreements.

events.title: MH17 shot down
events.text: A Buk missile from Russia's 53rd Anti-Aircraft Brigade destroyed Malaysia Airlines flight 17 over the Donbas, killing 298 people; a Dutch court convicted three men in absentia in 2022.

events.title: Russian build-up and demands
events.text: Russia massed some 190,000 troops on Ukraine's borders and in Belarus through late 2021 and demanded that NATO never admit Ukraine, while denying any plan to attack.

events.title: The full-scale invasion begins
events.text: Putin announced a 'special military operation' and missiles struck cities across Ukraine as columns crossed from Belarus, Russia and Crimea. Airborne troops seized Hostomel airfield near Kyiv and were thrown back within a day.

events.title: Bayraktar TB2 drones strike the columns
events.text: Ukraine's Turkish-built TB2 drones struck vehicle columns, supply lorries and air defence vehicles in the opening weeks, and the general staff published the footage. The slow, medium-altitude drone worked while Russian air defence was thin and disorganised; its usefulness fell away later in 2022 as that defence thickened.

events.title: The battle for Kyiv is won
events.text: Russian columns stalled north of Kyiv under ambushes, Javelins, artillery and their own logistics failures; by the end of March Russia announced a withdrawal from the north.

events.title: Bucha and the northern withdrawal
events.text: Ukrainian forces re-entering Bucha, Irpin and Borodianka found hundreds of murdered civilians. The evidence ended early peace talks in Istanbul and hardened Western support.

events.title: The cruiser Moskva sinks
events.text: Two Ukrainian Neptune missiles hit the Black Sea Fleet flagship, which sank the next day, the largest warship lost in combat since 1982.

events.title: Mariupol falls after Azovstal
events.text: After nearly three months of siege and the destruction of most of the city, the last defenders at the Azovstal steelworks surrendered on orders from Kyiv. Tens of thousands of civilians are believed to have died.

events.title: HIMARS enters the war
events.text: American HIMARS launchers began destroying Russian ammunition depots and bridges up to 80 kilometres behind the line, ending the artillery advantage that had taken Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk.

events.title: Kharkiv counteroffensive
events.text: Ukrainian forces broke through thin Russian lines east of Kharkiv, took Balakliia, Kupiansk and Izium in a week and recovered most of the oblast, the war's fastest advance.

events.title: Russia announces mobilisation
events.text: Putin ordered the call-up of 300,000 reservists, the first Russian mobilisation since 1945; hundreds of thousands of men left the country and the annexation of four oblasts was proclaimed nine days later.

events.title: The Crimean Bridge is hit
events.text: A truck bomb collapsed part of the road bridge to Crimea; Russia answered with the first mass missile strikes on Ukraine's energy system, opening the winter campaign against the grid.

events.title: Kherson liberated
events.text: Cut off by HIMARS strikes on the Dnipro bridges, Russian forces withdrew from the only regional capital they had captured; Ukrainian troops entered the city to crowds in the streets.

events.title: Winter strikes on the power grid
events.text: Waves of cruise missiles and Shahed drones through the winter of 2022 to 2023 left millions without power and heat, without breaking the grid or public support.

events.title: Western tanks pledged
events.text: Germany, the United States and European partners agreed to send Leopard 2, Abrams and Challenger 2 tanks after months of hesitation, followed by Patriot batteries and, in May, Storm Shadow missiles.

events.title: Storm Shadow cruise missiles arrive
events.text: The United Kingdom confirmed it had supplied Storm Shadow air-launched cruise missiles, the first Western weapon able to reach several hundred kilometres behind the front. France followed with the near-identical SCALP. Strikes on headquarters, depots and bridges in occupied territory and in Crimea began within days.

events.title: Bakhmut falls to Wagner
events.text: After ten months of the war's longest battle, Wagner's prisoner-recruited assault groups took the ruined city at a cost estimated in the tens of thousands of casualties on each side.

events.title: Kakhovka dam destroyed
events.text: The dam on the Dnipro collapsed while under Russian control, flooding towns downstream, killing dozens and draining the reservoir that cooled the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant.

events.title: The 2023 counteroffensive begins
events.text: Ukraine's new brigades attacked towards Melitopol and Berdiansk into dense minefields covered by Ka-52 helicopters and Lancets; Robotyne was taken in August but no breakthrough followed.

events.title: Wagner mutiny
events.text: Yevgeny Prigozhin's Wagner columns seized Rostov-on-Don and drove towards Moscow before a deal halted them; Prigozhin died in a plane crash two months later.

events.title: Black Sea Fleet headquarters struck
events.text: Storm Shadow missiles destroyed the fleet headquarters in Sevastopol; with a submarine and landing ship hit in dry dock and naval drones stalking the harbour, most of the fleet moved to Novorossiysk.

events.title: First ATACMS strikes
events.text: Secretly delivered ATACMS missiles destroyed helicopters at Berdiansk and Luhansk airfields, and Ukraine's counteroffensive was acknowledged to have stalled by November.

events.title: The commander-in-chief calls it a stalemate
events.text: Valerii Zaluzhnyi told The Economist that the war had reached a positional stalemate and that no deep breakthrough was likely without new technology to answer drones, mines and electronic warfare. Zelenskyy's office publicly disagreed with the assessment, and the disagreement ran on until Zaluzhnyi was replaced in February 2024.

events.title: US support stalls in Congress
events.text: The White House told Congress that money for Ukraine had run out, and a supplemental package was then held for six months in a dispute over American border policy. Shell rationing at the front through the winter and spring followed, and Avdiivka fell during it. Support from Washington became a matter of argument rather than a given.

events.title: Zaluzhnyi replaced by Syrskyi
events.text: President Zelenskyy replaced the popular commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi with Oleksandr Syrskyi after months of reported disputes over mobilisation and strategy.

events.title: Avdiivka falls
events.text: After four months of assault under glide bombs and with Ukrainian ammunition rationed while US aid was blocked in Congress, Ukraine withdrew from the fortress town it had held since 2014.

events.title: US aid resumes
events.text: Congress passed a 61 billion dollar package after a six-month blockage; ammunition and the 300-kilometre ATACMS reached the front within weeks. Ukraine also lowered its mobilisation age to 25.

events.title: Russian incursion north of Kharkiv
events.text: Russia opened a new front towards Vovchansk and Lyptsi, drawing Ukrainian reserves; it was contained within weeks and led allies to permit strikes into Russia near the border.

events.title: F-16s arrive
events.text: The first European F-16s entered Ukrainian service, initially against cruise missiles and drones; one was lost with its pilot in the first weeks.

events.title: Ukraine invades Kursk Oblast
events.text: Ukrainian brigades crossed the border and took Sudzha and some 1,000 square kilometres in days, the first foreign occupation of Russian territory since 1945; the salient held until spring 2025.

events.title: North Korean troops enter combat
events.text: Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers deployed to Kursk engaged Ukrainian forces from early November, confirmed by Kyiv, Seoul and Washington; two were captured in January 2025.

events.title: Oreshnik fired at Dnipro
events.text: Days after Ukraine's first ATACMS and Storm Shadow strikes inside Russia, Russia fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile with inert warheads at Dnipro as a signal to the West.

events.title: Washington changes course
events.text: The new US administration opened direct talks with Moscow, clashed publicly with Zelenskyy in the Oval Office and briefly paused aid and intelligence; Ukraine accepted a 30-day ceasefire proposal in March that Russia declined.

events.title: Kursk salient largely lost
events.text: Russian and North Korean forces, using fibre-optic drones against Ukrainian supply routes, retook Sudzha in March and most of the salient by late April.

events.title: Operation Spiderweb
events.text: FPV drones smuggled into Russia in lorry roofs struck strategic bombers on airfields from Murmansk to Irkutsk; Ukraine claimed 41 aircraft hit, US officials fewer. The operation exposed the bomber fleet to drones for the first time.

events.title: Russia's summer offensive
events.text: Russian forces pushed on Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka and into Sumy and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts through the summer with small infantry groups and motorcycles, gaining ground slowly at heavy cost without a breakthrough.

events.title: Campaign against Russian refineries
events.text: Ukrainian long-range drones hit a large share of Russia's major refineries repeatedly through 2025, cutting output and causing fuel shortages in Russian regions; Russia answered with record Shahed and missile waves on Ukraine's grid.

events.title: The 28-point plan
events.text: A US 28-point peace plan, read as close to Russian terms, prompted counter-drafts from Kyiv and European capitals; Moscow rejected the revised versions and fighting continued.

events.title: Four years of full-scale war
events.text: On the fourth anniversary Zelenskyy put Ukrainian military deaths at about 55,000 with many more missing, a figure independent trackers consider low; estimates of Russian dead from named-casualty counts run far higher. All such figures are contested.

events.title: Command crisis in Kyiv
events.text: Amid protests over the defence ministry and the conduct of the war, Zelenskyy replaced Oleksandr Syrskyi with Mykhailo Drapatyi as commander-in-chief in July 2026 (reported; see current updates for later changes).
